fr:title.text: The Computer Scientist's Approach to Proposition and Proof

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Computer Scientist's Approach to Proposition and Proof

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: Some software or computer logic is both highly technical and explicitly mathematical. Depending on the level of computation, the goal of a bit of code—maybe something backing a zero-knowledge proof or the design of a chip—may be extremely easy to state precisely because the purpose of the software is expressly technical and/or mathematical. In these cases, the specification tends to be abundantly clear because the work of settling on the correct definition and desired behavior of things was solved mathematically before it was translated into software.

At these higher layers of abstraction, software can become difficult to specify correctly. By this I mean that the intended and desired behavior of software can be difficult to articulate in prose or in formal language.

Consider the problem of specifying the "correct" behavior of a large language model like Chat GPT. The technologists who have built these LLMs are probably more aware than anyone—no one really knows what the correct behavior of an artificial intelligence is or should be. We want it to be helpful, knowledgeable, and honest—yes, but there are also some things we would rather it not produce even though it could do so in principle within the bounds of being helpful, knowledgeable, and honest. These things include somewhat-universally-agreed-upon things like child porn and slanderous and libelous deep fakes. In more of a grey area, they increasingly also include politically inconvenient facts or references to certain events in history about which we remain sensitive.

In other words, we want the LLM to be kind, or to have a value system of some kind. An LLM should not encourage someone to kill themselves. It shouldn't help someone build a bomb. It shouldn't help someone plan to commit a crime (although .. maybe it should help a revolutionary overthrow a tyrant?).

The problem with asking an LLM to behave ethically is who is to say what is right, and good, and true? What value system should dominate? People will have different philosophies on what they think the behavior of an LLM should be, but we are far from any point of consensus on what that should be. Yes, most of us want an LLM to align with what is good, virtuous, and true; the problem is that it is hard to know what is good, virtuous, and true, and thus hard to train an AI to align itself with that. (Think of the film I, Robot as a meditation on the unintended (and disasterous, tyranical) consequences of instilling a seemingly straightforward and simple value system into an intelligent robot.)

I would argue that the problem of correctly specifying an LLM is the problem that religion tends to address—one of value, meaning, and knowing goodness. This is an ancient problem, one that I would argue is so nuanced and complex that it can barely be told in story form—much less in prose, and even less a formal specification.
The specification of LLMs may be intractable, but I think we can make progress in something less, say, human: smart contracts.

fr:title.text: Proposition and Proof in Mathematics and Computer Science

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Proposition and Proof in Mathematics and Computer Science

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: Proof assistants are one link by which the notions of proposition and proof are relevant to computer scientists and mathematicians alike. Computer scientists use proof assistants, such as Coq or Lean, to formally verify code whose security is paramount by stating and proving theorems. Mathematicians increasingly use proof assistants in a project to formalize both classical and modern mathematics.

However, proposition and proof for mathematicians and computer scientists often do not much resemble each other, both in how proofs are engineered as well as in the kinds of propositions formalized. Unless software specifications are explicitly mathematical, like in the case of zero-knowledge proofs, computer scientists typically formalize properties from a prose specification into a set of propositions and prove code correct with regards to that specification by proving those propositions true. These sorts of propositions comprising the specification are informed by experience and best practices, but typically not any formal, underlying theory. In contrast, the propositions posed by mathematicians draw completely on the theory in which new propositions are couched, and the statements of propositions are derived in a methodical and highly rigorous manner.

These differences are, in my mind, well worth meditating on. My PhD was in some ways an attempt to reconcile the mathematical approach to stating and proving theorems; the jury is still out for me as to whether that is actually useful.

Smart contracts are programs stored on a blockchain that automatically execute when certain predefined conditions are met. Financial smart contracts are broadly defined as smart contracts that serve as a digital intermediary between financial parties. These include contracts collectively referred to as decentralized finance (DeFi), and come in many forms, including decentralized exchanges (DEXs), automated market makers (AMMs), crypto lending, synthetics (including stablecoins), yield farming, crypto insurance protocols, and cross-chain bridges. Financial smart contracts frequently manage huge quantities of money, making it essential for the underlying code to be rigorously tested and verified to ensure its correctness and security.
